name: Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia
info: The Armenian state founded in Cilicia by refugees from the Seljuk conquest, a kingdom from 1198, ally of Crusaders and Mongols and hub of Mediterranean trade until the Mamluks destroyed it in 1375.

facts.capital: Tarsus, then Sis (moved by Thoros I, c. 1100)
facts.founder: Ruben, who founded the Rubenid principality in 1080; Levon I, crowned the first king on 6 January 1198
facts.predecessor: Byzantine Cilicia and the principality of Philaretos Brachamios (1078–1085), settled by refugees from Bagratid Armenia
facts.successor: The Mamluk Sultanate (conquest of 1375); the royal title passed to James I of Cyprus in 1396

t: Ruben's revolt against Byzantium in 1080 founded the principality; Levon II's coronation at Tarsus on 6 January 1198, backed by the Holy Roman Emperor, made it a kingdom.
Het'um I's alliance with the Mongols, sealed at Karakorum in 1250 and 1253, drew Mamluk vengeance: Sis was sacked in 1266 and 40,000 Armenians carried off.
Cilician society adopted Western feudalism, chivalry and French titles, and the Armenian alphabet gained two letters, Ֆ and Օ, from the contact.
dyk: Marco Polo set out on his journey to China in 1271 from Ayas, the Cilician Armenian port where the Genoese held licensed warehouses and Italian was the language of trade.
ev: Ruben, a noble close to the murdered Bagratid king Gagik II, raises Armenian troops against the Byzantine Empire and founds the principality of Cilicia.
Prince Levon II is crowned King Levon I in the cathedral of Tarsus on 6 January, with a banner from Henry VI, Holy Roman Emperor; Cilician Armenia becomes a kingdom.
Queen Zabel is forced to marry Het'um, son of the regent Constantine of Baberon; as Het'um I he unites the rival Rubenid and Het'umid houses.
Het'um I visits Möngke Khan at Karakorum, confirming the Armeno-Mongol alliance his brother Smbat negotiated in 1247–1250.
Mamluk forces under Al-Mansur Ali and Qalawun overrun the Armenians at the Disaster of Mari, sack and burn Sis, massacre thousands and take 40,000 captives.
Het'um II joins the Mongol khan Ghazan to defeat the Mamluks at the Battle of Wadi al-Khazandar on 23 December.
The Mongol representative Bularghu murders King Levon III, the former king Het'um II and their party outside Anazarba; Oshin drives him out and becomes king.
Sis falls to the Mamluks, then the fortress of Gaban where King Levon V had taken refuge; the kingdom ends and Levon dies in exile in Paris in 1393.

sections.foundation:
The Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia was built by refugees. After Nicephorus II Phocas retook Cilicia from the Arabs in 965 the Byzantines settled Christians from Syria and Armenia there. More followed the Byzantine annexation of Greater Armenia in 1045 and its conquest by the Seljuk Turks nineteen years later: after Manzikert in 1071 Malik-Shah's governors laid repressive taxes on the Armenians, who fled west. Some Armenian leaders set themselves up as lords; the most successful, the former Byzantine general Philaretos Brachamios, held between 1078 and 1085 a principality from Malatia to Antioch and from Cilicia to Edessa; it crumbled before his death in 1090.

One of those nobles was Ruben, close to the last Bagratid king Gagik II, who was forced to cede his lands and assassinated by Greeks. In 1080, soon after, Ruben raised a band of Armenian troops and revolted against the Byzantine Empire, joined by many Armenian lords; the principality of Cilicia was founded under his leadership, and his descendants were the Rubenids. On his death in 1095 his son Constantine I ruled from the family fortresses, contending with the Het'umids founded by the former Byzantine general Oshin. The First Crusade gave Constantine powerful allies: the Armenians supplied the Crusaders with horses, provisions and guidance, and with their help cleared the remaining Byzantine strongholds. Thoros I, who succeeded around 1100, moved the capital from Tarsus to Sis.
sections.socioeconomy:
Cilician Armenia grew rich on its position at the junction of routes linking Central Asia and the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. It traded in spices, hides, wool and cotton and exported timber, grain, wine and raw silk. King Levon I made agreements with Pisa, Genoa and Venice and with the French and Catalans, granting tax exemptions in return for their business, and European merchant colonies settled in the kingdom; Italian became the second language of commerce as French was of the nobility. The chief harbours were the fortified coastal sites of Ayas and Korikos and the river emporium of Mopsuestia on the Pyramus. Marco Polo set out for China from Ayas in 1271. From the thirteenth century the kingdom struck its own gold and silver coins, the dram and tagvorin, at Sis and Tarsus.

The population was mixed: Armenians formed the ruling class beside Greeks, Jews, Muslims and various Europeans. Society moved from the traditional nakharar system towards Western feudalism; the titles baron and constable replaced nakharar and sparapet, nobles were knighted in the European manner, and the Armenian alphabet gained two letters, Ֆ and Օ, with Latin-based words. Ordinary Armenians were less won over, and most frowned on conversion to Roman Catholicism or Greek Orthodoxy. The Church ran through the land: the Catholicos, assisted by fourteen bishops under Levon I, sat at Hromkla from 1149 and at Sis after 1293, with up to sixty monasteries.
sections.military:
The kingdom lived behind castles. Rubenid fortresses from the Taurus Mountains into the plain and the Het'umid castles of Lampron and Baberon guarded its approaches. Early wars were against Byzantium and the Seljuks: Thoros I took Cyzistra in 1112 and killed the Byzantine brothers who had murdered Gagik II; John II reconquered the Cilician plain in 1137 and carried Levon I and his sons to Constantinople, but Thoros II escaped in 1141 and held off the Byzantines until he paid homage to Manuel I in 1158.

From 1247 the Het'umids staked everything on the Mongols. Smbat's embassy to Karakorum brought back in 1250 a guarantee of Cilicia's integrity; Het'um I visited Möngke Khan in 1253 and fought under Hulagu at Aleppo and Damascus in 1259–1260, where Arab historians charge his troops with a massacre and arson in the main mosque. The Mamluks answered. When Baibars summoned Het'um to change allegiance in 1266 and the king went to the Il-Khan for help, Al-Mansur Ali and Qalawun overran the outnumbered Armenians at the Disaster of Mari, killing Prince T'oros, capturing Levon, sacking and burning Sis, massacring thousands and carrying off 40,000 captives. In 1275 the emirs took Tarsus, burnt the palace, killed 15,000 civilians and took 10,000 to Egypt; almost all of Ayas's people perished. The truce of 1285 cost fortresses and a million dirhams a year, yet the raids went on, and Hromkla was sacked in 1292.
sections.governance:
For its first century Cilicia was a principality whose rulers Byzantium would not recognise as kings. Prince Levon II, who acceded in 1187, changed that: with the support of the Holy Roman Emperors Frederick Barbarossa and Henry VI he was crowned in the cathedral of Tarsus on 6 January 1198, the Armenian Christmas, by the Catholicos Gregory VI Abirad. His designs on Antioch provoked the Antiochene Wars of Succession. In 1219 his daughter Zabel was proclaimed ruler under the regent Adam of Baghras; when he was assassinated the regency went to Constantine of Baberon, a Het'umid, who married her to Bohemond IV's son Philip. Philip, too Latin for Armenian taste and accused of stealing the crown jewels, was imprisoned at Sis in 1224 and poisoned; Zabel was forced in 1226 to marry Constantine's son Het'um, who became co-ruler as Het'um I, uniting the two rival houses.

The Het'umids ruled through abdications and monasticism until Levon IV was killed by an angry mob in 1341 and the crown passed in 1342 to his cousin Guy de Lusignan as Constantine II. Religion was never settled: the Catholicos Grigor VI Apirat proclaimed union with Rome in 1198 to no effect, and the Armenian delegate Mkhitar Skewratsi asked at Acre in 1261 whence Rome drew “the power to pass judgment on the other Apostolic sees”. The Lusignans' drive to Latinise the Church was accepted by the nobles but resisted by the peasantry, and civil strife followed.
sections.impact:
Cilicia kept Armenian statehood alive while the Armenian highlands lay under foreign rule, and it became the focus of Armenian cultural production. The Catholicosate followed its people, settling at Hromkla in 1149 and Sis in 1293; the illuminated manuscripts of Toros Roslin, working at Hromkla, are among the finest Armenian art. The kingdom saw itself as a bastion of Christendom in the East and was the Crusaders' closest ally: Pope Gregory XIII later wrote that no people came to the Crusaders' aid “with the same enthusiasm, joy and faith as the Armenians did”. Intermarriage bound Armenian and Frankish houses, and Armenian castle-building, with its rocky heights, curved walls and round towers, passed through Armenian masons into Crusader castles such as Krak des Chevaliers and Marqab.

The Armeno-Mongol alliance Het'um I forged in 1247–1253 made Cilicia a partner in Hulagu's conquest of Syria and in Ghazan's campaigns of 1299–1303, and a target of the Mamluks. In return the West changed Armenian society: chivalry, French titles, names and language, feudal ranks and two new letters. After the fall, 30,000 wealthy Armenians moved to Lusignan Cyprus and merchant families founded or joined diaspora communities in France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain. The Holy See of Cilicia survives at Antelias in Lebanon, and the lion, emblem of the Cilician state, stands on the coat of arms of Armenia today.
sections.decline:
The Mongol alliance that had protected Cilicia failed it in the fourteenth century as the Crusader states and the Ilkhanate disintegrated. In 1307 Bularghu, the Mongol representative in Cilicia and a recent convert to Islam, murdered King Levon III, the former king Het'um II and their party; Oshin drove him out and the Ilkhan Oljeitu executed him, but the kingdom had lost its ally. The Het'umids ruled an unstable country until an angry mob killed Levon IV in 1341. In 1342 his cousin Guy de Lusignan was anointed Constantine II, and he and his brother John set out to impose Catholicism and European ways on a Church and peasantry that refused them, so civil strife divided the kingdom just as the Mamluks invaded again in 1343–1344.

Appeals to Europe and plans for new crusades brought nothing. Sis fell to the Mamluks, and in 1375 the fortress of Gaban, where King Levon V had taken refuge, fell too, ending the kingdom. Levon V was given safe passage and went to Castile to seek John I's help, moved to France and died in exile in Paris in 1393; in 1396 his title passed to his cousin James I of Cyprus. Turkic tribes settled Cilicia and Timur's conquest followed. Thirty thousand wealthy Armenians left for Cyprus, while humbler Armenians stayed through Turkic and Ottoman rule, and Cilicia remained one of the most Armenian regions of the Ottoman Empire until the massacre of Cilician Armenians at Adana in 1909.

summary: Founded in 1080 by Ruben, an Armenian lord in revolt against Byzantium, and made a kingdom when Levon I was crowned at Tarsus in 1198, Cilician Armenia was the Crusaders' ally and the Mongols' partner, grew rich on the trade of Ayas, and was worn down by Mamluk invasions and religious strife until Sis and Gaban fell in 1375.
references: T. S. R. Boase, The Cilician Kingdom of Armenia (Scottish Academic Press, 1978)
Jacob G. Ghazarian, The Armenian kingdom in Cilicia during the Crusades (Routledge, 2000)
Richard G. Hovannisian and Simon Payaslian (eds.), Armenian Cilicia (Mazda Publishers, 2008)
Frédéric Luisetto, Arméniens et autres Chrétiens d'Orient sous la domination Mongole (Geuthner, 2007)
Jean-Pierre Mahé, L'Arménie à l'épreuve des siècles (Gallimard, 2005)

pointDescs.1080: Ruben raises Armenian troops against the Byzantine Empire after Gagik II's murder and founds the Rubenid principality of Cilicia, joined by many Armenian lords.
pointDescs.1100: Thoros I succeeds Constantine I, who had cleared the Byzantine garrisons with the First Crusade's help; he moves the capital from Tarsus to Sis.
pointDescs.1112: Thoros I takes the castle of Cyzistra and kills the three Byzantine brothers who had assassinated Gagik II.
pointDescs.1129: Levon I begins his reign and integrates the Cilician coastal cities, consolidating Armenian commercial leadership in the region.
pointDescs.1137: Emperor John II conquers most of the Cilician plain and imprisons Levon I and his sons in Constantinople, where Levon dies and Ruben is blinded and killed.
pointDescs.1141: Thoros II escapes from Constantinople, returns to Cilicia and leads the struggle against the Byzantines, repelling their invasions.
pointDescs.1158: Thoros II pays homage to Emperor Manuel I in a short-lived treaty; the Catholicos has moved his see to Hromkla around 1151.
pointDescs.1187: Prince Levon II accedes, fights the Seljuks of Iconium, Aleppo and Damascus, doubles the Mediterranean coastline and courts the Europeans during the Third Crusade.
pointDescs.1198: Levon II is crowned King Levon I at Tarsus on 6 January with the support of Henry VI; he grants privileges to Pisa, Genoa and Venice and the economy prospers.
pointDescs.1226: Het'um I becomes co-ruler with Queen Zabel, uniting the Rubenid and Het'umid houses after a century of rivalry.
pointDescs.1250: Smbat returns from Karakorum with a Mongol guarantee of Cilicia's integrity; Het'um I builds castles such as Tamrut, visits Möngke in 1253 and recovers Marash and Behesni.
pointDescs.1266: The Mamluks overrun Cilicia in Het'um's absence at the Disaster of Mari: T'oros is killed, Levon captured, Sis sacked and burnt, thousands massacred and 40,000 taken captive.
pointDescs.1275: Mamluk emirs take Tarsus, burn the palace and Saint Sophia, kill 15,000 civilians and carry 10,000 to Egypt; almost all of Ayas's people perish.
pointDescs.1285: After the defeat at the Second Battle of Homs in 1281, a ten-year truce forces the Armenians to cede fortresses, leave their defences unbuilt and pay a million dirhams a year.
pointDescs.1299: Het'um II joins Ghazan to defeat the Mamluks at Wadi al-Khazandar on 23 December, but the Mongols are beaten at Homs and Shaqhab in 1303, the last great Mongol invasion of Syria.
pointDescs.1307: Bularghu murders Levon III and Het'um II at Anazarba; Oshin avenges them and is crowned, but the kingdom is left without a regional ally.
pointDescs.1341: Levon IV is assassinated by an angry mob; the crown passes in 1342 to Guy de Lusignan as Constantine II, whose Latinising policy splits the kingdom.
pointDescs.1375: Sis and then Gaban fall to the Mamluks; Levon V goes into exile and the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia ends.

notes: The article numbers the rulers twice: Prince Levon II became King Levon I in 1198, and the later kings Levon II (1269), Levon III, IV and V follow the royal count; the profile uses the article's forms in each context.
The 1129 point rests on the article's statement that Prince Levon I 'integrated the Cilician coastal cities'; no other date is given for that.
The article does not date the fall of Sis separately from Gaban (1375); the last event and point say Sis fell, then Gaban in 1375.
Het'um I's part in the Aleppo massacre of 1260 is reported as the article does, with the debate over the Templar of Tyre's account left out for space.
The article's Further reading lists Stubbs's 1886 lectures and an Armenian Soviet Encyclopedia entry as well; five works are given.
